A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SWEET research, with matching methods, benchmarks, and main contributions. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original SWEET and ensemble evaluations on Arabic GEC benchmarks, edit-representation experiments, LLM evaluations, and measured runtimes.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds error-type performance analysis and corpus error distributions.

M1.justification: The edit extraction, compression, subword projection, punctuation segregation, pruning, iterative correction, and ensemble voting procedures remain unchanged. Renaming '+ GPT-4o' to '4-Ensemble' does not introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions use QALB-2014, QALB-2015 L1, ZAEBUC, and MADAR CODA, covering the same MSA tasks and five city dialects. The added error analysis examines existing data; revised corpus counts do not establish new coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Appendix E expands comparisons beyond the best-per-dataset Seq2Seq++ summaries, reporting additional AraT5/AraBART variants with morphological preprocessing and GED features in Tables 12–13. The LLM comparator set is retained, while Appendix F mainly identifies the existing DA baselines more explicitly.

E3.justification: V2 adds error-type and macro F0.5 evaluation and expands the documented five-shot prompts in Figure 3. Table 2 revises MADAR CODA word totals from 25K/5K/5K to 40K/9K/9K, retaining sentence counts and stated splits. These reported revisions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section 5.1 systematically compares the best Seq2Seq++ baseline, SWEET setup, and four-model ensemble across error types on three development sets. Table 7 supplies category-specific performance, supported by splitwise error distributions in Appendix G. This adds a substantial diagnostic analysis beyond the retained representation, pruning, and prompting experiments.

E5.justification: V1 provides point scores without significance tests. V2 introduces two-sided approximate randomization testing, p < 0.05 judgments, and significance annotations across the principal benchmark comparisons. Seed 42 and ten runtime repetitions were already documented; the revision does not establish additional training runs. Some duplicated significance annotations disagree.

E6.justification: The primary benchmark score entries remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial diagnostic results. Table 7 reports ZAEBUC macro F0.5 of 71.2 for cascaded SWEET, 66.7 for the baseline, and 63.1 for the ensemble, revealing a ranking different from overall GEC performance. Additional baseline-variant scores, error distributions, significance findings, and revised corpus counts and error rates further expand the reported evidence.

T1.justification: The sequence-tagging formulation, edit definitions, alignment description, and ensemble voting rule are retained. Neither version adds theoretical results or proofs, and the new empirical error-type evaluation introduces no substantive mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: data-derived edits without language-specific rules, successful Arabic text editing, SOTA results on two benchmarks and comparable results on two others, faster inference, and ensemble gains. Added statistical qualifications appear in the results discussion without changing these headline claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains differences between aggregate and error-type rankings through error-frequency imbalance and precision–recall tradeoffs. It also identifies ARETA's limitations for dialect-specific errors and explicitly qualifies SWEET's small DA advantage as statistically insignificant. The existing Limitations section remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendices E–F identify the architectures and feature variants behind generic Seq2Seq baseline labels. Figure 3 expands prompt-template documentation, including example framing, output formatting, and final-query instructions. Training hyperparameters, hardware, and code/data/model access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Magdy et al. (2024), Gazelle, to the Arabic GEC background and Belkebir and Habash (2021), ARETA, for error annotation. These are limited citation additions; the central positioning relative to earlier text-editing and Arabic GEC research is retained.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose edits, renames the GPT-4o-augmented ensemble, adds an affiliation and acknowledgments, and inserts an Error Analysis subsection. Additional appendices move Prompts from Appendix E to H. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with error-type performance and distribution tables plus four appendix benchmark tables that expose baseline variants or redisplay existing results. Existing benchmark tables gain significance symbols and explanatory captions, and the prompt figures are reformatted and expanded. The method figure and basic document style are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 provides useful diagnostic evidence, clearer baseline and prompt documentation, and corrected MADAR word counts while preserving the main score entries. Statistical qualifications make the small DA gain easier to assess. These benefits are limited by conflicting significance annotations in Tables 3/12 and 6/15, and by expanded prompt templates without clarification of whether the unchanged LLM results were rerun.
